lines.name: South Bay Line

segments.constraint: Posted 5 mph area in South San Diego Bay south of Loews Resort / Sweetwater Channel (pylon-marked wildlife-refuge water) caps the first ~2–3 nm out of Chula Vista
segments.routing: Exit Safe Harbor South Bay at marina speed and hold the marked channel north through the posted South Bay 5 mph zone (cement pylons; wildlife refuges, sea-turtle habitat and shoals outside the channel) until clear of Loews Resort / Sweetwater Channel; then full-speed main-channel water up the central bay — passing under the Coronado Bridge navigation span, standing clear of the Bay Bridge mooring/roadstead 5 mph area, the 33 CFR 165.1101 security-zone shore off 32nd St, and §334.880 naval anchorages — to the Fifth Avenue Landing approach.

Short main-channel hop along the downtown Embarcadero; no general speed limit in the main channel (SDUPD Port Code §4.35(c)(3)); mind cruise-ship movements at B Street Pier and harbor-tour traffic; marina/berth speeds at the pier faces only.

lines.phase_notes: Flagship corridor. ~30–40 min Chula Vista↔downtown indicative end-to-end INCLUDING the 5 mph South Bay tail, vs a 15–60 min I-5 drive. Anchored by Gaylord Pacific (walking distance from the Chula Vista landing) on the reverse commute + downtown/Convention Center employers on the forward run. The demand signal is brand new and proven — a public commuter ferry launched on this exact pair June 1, 2026 — and Navier's employer seat-block overlay adds guaranteed seats and frequency as a complement to it, never a displacement (incumbent_respect_flagship governs all copy).

lines.name: Point Loma Line

segments.constraint: Short basin-to-basin hop dominated by Shelter Island / America's Cup Harbor basin and marina speed limits — no meaningful open-water segment
segments.routing: Round the Shelter Island mole between the guest docks and America's Cup Harbor at basin speeds; all inside-basin water.

Exit America's Cup Harbor and run the north-bay main channel east: full-speed water (no general main-channel limit, SDUPD §4.35(c)(3)); stay in/near the marked channel clear of the Point Loma naval-shore zones (33 CFR 165.1102; §334.870 degaussing-station most-direct-transit rule) and the §334.880 anchorage; enter the Harbor Island basin at marina speed.
Short full-speed hop from the Harbor Island basin east along the main channel to the Broadway Pier face; marina-basin speeds on exit only.

lines.phase_notes: Phase 2 premium residential play: the highest verified catchment income in the market (Point Loma 92106, $142,897) into the downtown core, ~15–25 min indicative, essentially all full-speed water — and NO incumbent scheduled service exists on this pair. Harbor Island is the authored opportunistic infill stop; it carries no airport story (see its note_internal — the 2025 entrance road already solved most of that pain, and no landing serves the terminals).

lines.name: Bridge Line

segments.constraint: 5 mph inside Glorietta Bay (SDUPD Port Code §4.35(c)(3)) plus the Bay Bridge mooring/roadstead 5 mph area on the crossing
segments.routing: Exit Glorietta Bay at 5 mph, pass through the Coronado Bridge navigation span, cross the main channel standing clear of the Bay Bridge mooring/roadstead 5 mph area, and approach Fifth Avenue Landing at berth speed.

lines.phase_notes: Coronado Bridge bypass feeder — Coronado residents into the Convention Center / Gaslamp core without the bridge. Deliberately anchored at Glorietta Bay — NOT at the incumbent ferry's Coronado landing — to complement (not clone) the existing subsidized Coronado ferry (see decision_ledger). The crossing is below the 20-min sweet spot and partly speed-constrained — bundle as a feeder with NO numeric time claim; a City of Coronado / incumbent-partner conversation gates this line.

incumbent_respect_flagship.rule: Flagship Cruises & Events (family-owned, operating since 1915) runs the Coronado ferry (20 departures/day incl. free City-subsidized commuter runs 4:50–8:30 AM since 1993), the Convention Center↔Coronado shuttle every 30 min, the NEW Chula Vista↔Convention Center commuter ferry (June 1, 2026), an on-call water taxi — and has announced an electric ferry fleet for fall 2026. Flagship is the proof that San Diego commutes by water and a potential operating partner — NEVER positioned as a competitor and never disparaged. NO Broadway↔Coronado line exists in any phase (decision_ledger). Copy may cite the commuter-ferry precedent as market proof; Navier's framing is always employer-guaranteed seat blocks, new station pairs, and added frequency as a COMPLEMENT to existing service. Zero displacement, head-to-head, 'faster than the ferry', or comparison-table framing anywhere in rendered copy.
incumbent_respect_flagship.note: The South Bay Line shares the Chula Vista↔Convention Center pair with Flagship's 6x/day service — the overlay story there is guaranteed employer seats + commuter frequency, positioned additively. Partner-conversation posture is internal only.

south_bay_speed_honesty.rule: Segments flagged speed_constrained:true must render water_min as 'indicative — subject to San Diego Bay speed rules' — never a bare per-segment number. Whitelisted end-to-end indicative ranges (always with an 'indicative' qualifier): South Bay Line ~30–40 min Chula Vista↔downtown INCLUDING the 5 mph tail; Point Loma Line ~15–25 min. The Bridge Line renders NO numeric time claim (short + constrained feeder). Mid-bay honesty cuts both ways: the main channel and central bay have NO general speed limit for a passenger vessel (SDUPD Port Code §4.35(c)(3)) — never imply a bay-wide limit exists, and never hide the South Bay 5 mph tail from the time model.

navy_base_honesty.rule: No military base is served dockside, ever. Base docks are controlled (33 CFR 165.1101/165.1102/165.1103/165.1105; 33 CFR 334.870/334.880) and no civilian service can land on-base. NASNI-adjacent commuters are reachable only via public Coronado landings at bike/base-shuttle tier (mirroring how the existing free commuter ferry works); the 32nd St gates are shuttle-tier (~1.5–2 mi) from Pier 32 Marina, which is not routed. The shipyard shift-change market is unaddressable today and is watchlist-gated on a Cesar Chavez Park float. Rendered copy carries NO base names, NO installation headcounts, NO base-service claims, and NO security-zone material — only honest generic phrasing ('Coronado and South Bay employers'). All specifics live in note_internal / no_landing / decision_ledger, which never render.

port_single_landlord_internal.rule: The Port of San Diego (SDUPD) controls tidelands across all five bay cities — one landlord relationship unlocks nearly every landing (exceptions: Glorietta Bay Marina is City of Coronado; private club docks). Charter/commercial passenger ops from any marina require operator permission + Port process (SDUPD Code §4.37), and whether the Port would permit a second scheduled passenger operator at Broadway Pier / Fifth Avenue Landing is UNKNOWN — the first dock-track question. ALL of this is internal dock-track context: ZERO external mention of the Port as landlord, tideland permitting, §4.37, or operator-permission questions anywhere in rendered copy.

copy.hero: Your dock becomes a station on a connected water network. Navier is building an employer water network for San Diego Bay — 20-seat electric hydrofoils linking Chula Vista's new bayfront, the Convention Center, and downtown's Broadway Pier at launch, growing to Shelter Island, Point Loma, Harbor Island, and Glorietta Bay. One protected bay, twelve miles of fast water, and a commute that skips the bridge and the freeway.

sections.why_san_diego: San Diego's bayfront commute funnels through two chokepoints: the Coronado Bridge — roughly 75,000 vehicles a day, where a physical barrier still gets moved twice daily to flip a lane with the commute — and the I-5 South corridor, where a 15-minute free-flow drive from Chula Vista routinely stretches far longer at rush hour. The bay itself is the alternative: twelve nautical miles of protected water running straight past every major bayfront job cluster, with fast, open water in the main channel. And San Diego already commutes by water — a commuter ferry has crossed to Coronado every weekday morning for three decades, and a new Chula Vista run launched in 2026. The water works. We add guaranteed seats and new stations.
sections.how_it_works: Employers commit seat blocks on a corridor. When a corridor reaches 60–80 committed seats, it launches. Seats are guaranteed, quiet, working commutes on zero-emission electric hydrofoils.
sections.network: At launch, one flagship corridor: the South Bay Line — Chula Vista Bayfront · Convention Center (Fifth Avenue Landing) · Broadway Pier — about 30–40 minutes end to end (indicative), anchored by the Gaylord Pacific resort at walking distance from the Chula Vista landing. Phase 2 adds the Point Loma Line — Shelter Island · America's Cup Harbor · Harbor Island · Broadway Pier, about 15–25 minutes (indicative) — the bay's highest-income catchment, with no scheduled water service on that pair today. Phase 3 adds the Bridge Line, a Glorietta Bay ↔ Convention Center feeder giving Coronado a bridge-free crossing. Phase 2 and 3 stations render as planned, not promised.
sections.chula_vista_growth: Chula Vista's bayfront is the fastest-growing employer story on the bay. The Gaylord Pacific Resort & Convention Center opened in May 2025 with 1,600 rooms and roughly 800 hires at opening — and thousands more jobs are projected as the bayfront district builds out — all at walking distance from the water. Employer seat blocks there fill the reverse commute; downtown, Convention Center, and Gaslamp employers fill the forward run.
sections.working_with_the_ferry: San Diego's ferry operator has served this bay for over a century, and its commuter runs prove the market every weekday. Navier's network is designed as a complement — guaranteed employer seat blocks, new station pairs like Point Loma and Glorietta Bay, and more frequency where today's schedule is light — never a replacement.
sections.timing: Targeting first service no earlier than end-2027. Every travel time shown is indicative until routes are finalized with harbor authorities, and South Bay times include the posted slow-speed zone near Chula Vista.
sections.loi_ask: Register interest with a non-binding letter of intent. It costs nothing and reserves nothing — it tells us which corridors to launch first.
